questions.q: What does hemineglect do to patients like Ellen?
a: It makes one side of their surroundings seem not to exist
It makes them invent detailed memories of events
It makes them laugh at moments that are not funny
It makes them believe a paralyzed limb still works
questions.why: Lesson 1 says patients are blind to one side and act as if that side does not exist at all.

questions.q: Which area of the brain is damaged in hemineglect cases?
a: The right parietal lobe
The left frontal lobe
The limbic system
The brain stem
questions.why: Lesson 1 says these cases always follow a stroke in the right parietal lobe, an area that helps with perception.

questions.q: What is anosognosia, as described in the summary?
a: Denying a paralysis that brain damage has caused
Laughing uncontrollably after a brain injury
Failing to recognize people you know well
Seeing cartoon characters as real people
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes Mrs. Dodd insisting her paralyzed arm worked, a severe denial called anosognosia.

questions.q: What can happen after a stroke in the left hemisphere?
a: Patients become obsessed with being sick
Patients deny that anything is wrong
Patients neglect one half of their vision
Patients lose the ability to speak
questions.why: Lesson 2 notes that the opposite of denial, an obsession with illness, appears after left hemisphere strokes.

questions.q: How do evolutionary psychologists explain why laughter first developed?
a: As a signal that a perceived threat was a false alarm
As a way for groups to choose their leaders
As a method for teaching children safe behavior
As a bonding ritual used only during ceremonies
questions.why: Lesson 3 says early humans may have laughed to tell others that a threat turned out to be harmless.
